The query nodes A and B are outlined in the accent color, and both edges between them, ids 1 and 6, are highlighted. The card returns 1 and 6." width="100%"} Returns the IDs of every edge that joins the two given nodes, in the order the edges were added. Because edgecase graphs allow multi-edges (several edges between the same pair of nodes), the result can hold more than one ID. For undirected graphs, edges are matched regardless of the order in which their endpoints were given when added. For directed graphs, only edges running from `source=` to `target=` are returned. Passing the same node twice finds its self-loops. This is the bridge between "node pair" thinking and the edge-ID-based methods. Use it to: - look up the ID of an edge so you can read or modify it with `get_edge()`, set its attributes, or delete it with `delete_edge_by_id()` - list all parallel edges between two nodes (e.g. multiple flights between two cities) - count the multiplicity of a connection with `len(...)` If you only need a yes/no answer, `has_edge()` is simpler. The search covers the whole graph and ignores the current selection. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The first endpoint, as a node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). In a directed graph this is the node the edges must start from. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second endpoint, as a node ID (`int`) or label (`str`). In a directed graph this is the node the edges must point to. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The matching edge IDs in insertion order. Empty list if no edges join the nodes. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `source=` or `target=` is an ID or label that doesn't belong to any node. [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `source=` or `target=` is neither an `int` nor a `str`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Because multigraphs allow more than one edge between the same pair of nodes, `find_edge_ids()` returns every match rather than just the first: ::: {#fa25d4ec .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_nodes(["A", "B"]) graph.add_edges( [ ("A", "B"), ("A", "B"), # a second, parallel edge ] ) graph.find_edge_ids(source="A", target="B") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [1, 2] ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph the order of the endpoints matters. Asking for `B -> A` finds only the single reverse edge, and a pair with no edges gives an empty list: ::: {#09da0b16 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("A", "B"), ("B", "A")]) ) ( graph.find_edge_ids(source="A", target="B"), graph.find_edge_ids(source="B", target="A"), graph.find_edge_ids(source="A", target="C"), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ([1, 2], [3], []) ``` ::: ::: The returned IDs can be handed straight to edge-level methods. Here one of the two parallel `A -> B` edges is removed, leaving a single connection in that direction: ::: {#8eaabbd0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} first_id = graph.find_edge_ids(source="A", target="B")[0] graph.delete_edge_by_id(first_id) graph.find_edge_ids(source="A", target="B") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [2] ``` ::: :::
